overview.text: A volcanic eruption occurs when gases, rock fragments, and/or molten rock escape from within Earth through a vent. Molten rock underground is magma; after it reaches the surface, it is called lava. Eruptions range from relatively quiet outpourings of fluid lava to explosive blasts. Their style depends on magma’s composition, viscosity, gas content, and eruption rate: runny magma lets gas escape more easily, while sticky, gas-rich magma can build pressure and shatter into ash and larger fragments. Eruptions shape volcanic landforms, but lava, ash, hot fragment-laden clouds, and gases can threaten people and damage nearby areas. In major explosive eruptions, sulfur dioxide can form reflective sulfate aerosols high in the atmosphere, temporarily reducing sunlight and cooling climate.

key_facts.text: Magma is molten rock below Earth’s surface; once it erupts, it is called lava.
Effusive eruptions tend to produce lava flows or fountains with little ash; explosive eruptions can send large amounts of ash high into the atmosphere.
Magma composition, viscosity, gas content, and eruption rate help determine how explosive an eruption is.
Volcanic ash is made of small rock fragments; larger fragments may also be thrown out during explosive eruptions.
Large eruptions can send sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere, where it can form reflective sulfate aerosols that temporarily cool climate.
